basics.name: Free and public-domain machine design textbooks: FUNdaMENTALs of Design (Alexander Slocum, MIT), Introduction to Mechanical Design and Manufacturing (David Jensen, University of Arkansas open textbook), and Basic Machines (US Navy NAVPERS 10624 / 10624-A)
basics.url: Slocum: https://pergatory.mit.edu/resources/FUNdaMENTALS.html (chapter PDFs, e.g. https://pergatory.mit.edu/resources/FUNdaMENTALs%20Book%20pdf/FUNdaMENTALs%20Topic%206.PDF, and a whole-book zip). UArk: Open Textbook Library record https://open.umn.edu/opentextbooks/textbooks/introduction-to-mechanical-design-and-manufacturing, whose format links redirect to the book at https://uark.pressbooks.pub/mechanicaldesign/ (that host was blocked from this environment, so the book itself was not opened) [uncertain]. Navy: 1946 scan https://archive.org/details/BasicMachines10624 and the 1971 Dover reprint of the 1965 NAVPERS 10624-A edition https://archive.org/details/basicmachineshow00unit
basics.resource_type: book (three free textbooks; Slocum and Navy as PDF, UArk as an online Pressbooks book with PDF/eBook downloads); listed in the project as a digital library
basics.cost: Free (all three can be read or downloaded without payment); the Navy book is also sold in print as a Dover reprint (ISBN 0486217094)
basics.license: Slocum: all rights reserved ('Copyright 2008 Alexander Slocum' on every page; the MIT page says 'Copyright Massachusetts Institute of Technology All Rights Reserved'), free to download and link but not to copy figures. UArk: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial (CC BY-NC, per the Open Textbook Library record; version 4.0 per search listings [uncertain]), so text and figures can be reused non-commercially with credit. Navy: a US federal government work, so public domain in the US; the Internet Archive marks the 1946 scan with the Public Domain Mark 1.0, so text and diagrams can be copied freely. The 1965/1971 edition credits a few figures to outside sources (Underwood Corporation typewriter figures 12-4 to 12-16, US Naval Institute books), which may not be public domain [uncertain]
basics.year: Slocum: book copyright 2007, chapters dated 1 January 2008, web page updated 1 February 2008 (zip last modified April 2008); not updated since. UArk: copyright year 2024. Navy: first edition 1946 (NAVPERS 10624), revised 1965 (NAVPERS 10624-A, 15 chapters), Dover reprint 1971; the 1946 scan was uploaded to the Internet Archive in 2014
basics.access_barrier: none (direct PDF downloads for Slocum and the Navy book; UArk is open on Pressbooks, but its host was blocked from this research environment)
basics.image_license: Slocum: all rights reserved, and many collage photos appear to come from companies and websites, so do not copy [uncertain]. UArk: presumably CC BY-NC like the text, but individual figures may carry their own credits [uncertain]. Navy: public-domain line drawings (except the few credited third-party figures noted above)
basics.authority_level: educator (Slocum is an MIT professor, book written for MIT course 2.007; Jensen is a University of Arkansas professor, open textbook funded by the university libraries) and official government training manual (US Bureau of Naval Personnel); none is peer-reviewed research

coverage.covers: Slocum (10 topics, about 320 two-page spreads): design process, linkages (joints by degrees of freedom, 2-, 4-, 5-, 6-bar linkages, scissor linkages, compliant mechanisms and flexures), power transmission I (pulleys, capstans, winches, belts, cables, chains, wheels, clutches and differentials, cams, shafts, component attachment, interference fits, couplings), power transmission II (leadscrews, ballscrews, differential screws, preload, gears: involute, serial and planetary/epicyclic trains, differentials, spur, bevel, rack and pinion, worm), power systems (magnets, solenoids, motors, gearmotors, springs, pneumatics), structures, structural connections (welded, adhesive, bolted, pinned and riveted joints, Hertz contact, kinematic couplings, quasi-kinematic couplings, elastic averaging), bearings (sliding, rolling, flexural, hydrostatic, magnetic, preload, seals). UArk (16 parts): design process chapters plus 'Specification of Standard Mechanical Components', 'Assemblies for Motion and Power Delivery' (gears, bearings, linkages and mechanisms, mechanism synthesis per search listings) and manufacturing chapters including joining processes and fasteners (chapter contents seen only in search listings) [uncertain]. Navy 1946 (12 chapters): levers, block and tackle, wheel and axle, inclined plane, screw, gears, work, power, force and pressure, hydrostatic and hydraulic machines, complex machines. Navy 1965/1971 (15 chapters) adds machine elements and basic mechanisms (bearings, springs, couplings, cams, clutches, gear differential, typewriter ratchets, escapements and toggles), internal combustion engine, power trains (clutches, universal joints, differentials) and basic computer mechanisms (differentials, adding linkages, mechanical multipliers)
coverage.organisation: All three are textbooks organised in chapters by component family (linkages, power transmission, bearings, joints) or, for the Navy book, by the classical simple machines (lever, pulley, wheel and axle, inclined plane, screw, gears) building up to complex machines. None is organised by what the reader wants to do. Slocum's two-page spreads (text page plus a picture collage page) are designed for browsing by picture, which helps someone who does not know the terms; the Navy book uses everyday shipboard examples (hatch dogs, capstans, anchor winches) and plain language. Finding a specific connection type means using each chapter's table of contents
coverage.scope_match: medium: these are general machine-design texts, not catalogues of clever connections, but Slocum in particular covers many in-scope types (clutches, one-way springs, toggles, flexures, kinematic couplings, gear trains, solenoids, adhesives), and the 1965 Navy edition explains ratchets, detents, escapements, Oldham couplings and overrunning clutches in beginner language. The UArk book appears to be a more conventional survey of standard components [uncertain]
coverage.taxonomy_used: Slocum: 10 topics by design area (process, ideas, principles, linkages, power transmission I and II, power systems, structures, structural connections and interfaces, bearings); within linkages, joints are classed by degrees of freedom (single-DOF, multiple-DOF, higher pairs). Navy: the classical six simple machines (lever with 1st/2nd/3rd class, block and tackle, wheel and axle, inclined plane, screw, gears) plus physics chapters and 'complex machines' as combinations; the 1965 edition adds 'machine elements and basic mechanisms'. UArk: 16 parts following the design process and then manufacturing processes (casting and molding, forming and shaping, machining, joining, plastics)
coverage.example_types: Toggle (over-centre) clamping linkage; scissor (extending) linkage; compliant flexure mechanism, folded-beam flexure and bistable flexure; flexural pawl and ratchet (cable clamp); slip clutch with adjustable spring torque; one-way spring clutch (spring pressed over shaft ends); capstan with one-way clutch; interference (press) fit; low-cost pinned shaft coupling; differential leadscrew; non-backdriveable (self-locking) leadscrew; planetary (epicyclic) gear train; open differential; worm drive and non-reversing worm; rack and pinion; kinematic coupling (three-groove) and quasi-kinematic coupling; elastic averaging; adhesive joint geometries (lap, scarf, double strap); Oldham coupling; spiral jaw (ratchet-type) clutch and overrunning (sprag) clutch; ratchet-and-pawl platen drive and escapement; detent roller and spring; pelican hook (quick release); interrupted-screw breech plug (twist lock); hatch dog (lever plus wedge)
coverage.making_methods: General engineering and robotics (Slocum is written for the MIT 2.007 robot design contest and mentions FIRST robot teams; covers waterjet cutting and prototyping gears); UArk covers design for manufacturing and assembly with machining, casting, molding, forming, joining and plastic processes; Navy covers shipboard and workshop machinery. None is specific to 3D printing
coverage.item_count: Slocum: 10 topic chapters (about 30 to 39 two-page spreads each, about 320 in total) plus design spreadsheets for topics 3 to 11. UArk: 16 parts (chapter count not verified) [uncertain]. Navy: 12 chapters and about 157 pages (1946); 15 chapters and about 158 pages (1965/1971)
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: Torque-limiting: yes (Slocum's clutch page: rigid until a set torque, then slips; slip torque set by a spring screw; Navy clutches). Self-locking: yes (Slocum on backdriveability of leadscrews; Navy non-reversing worm drive). One-way/ratchet: yes (Slocum one-way spring clutch, flexural pawl/ratchet, capstan one-way clutch; Navy ratchet and pawl, spiral claw ratchet clutch, overrunning sprag clutch). Indexing/detent: yes in Navy 1965 (detent spring and detent roller, escapement) [uncertain for Slocum]. Over-centre: yes (Slocum toggle linkages and 5-bar clamping pliers; Navy typewriter shift toggle that 'moves slightly over center'). Compliant: yes, strongly in Slocum (flexures, compliant mechanisms, bistable flexures, flexural bearings). Hand-release only: partly (Navy pelican hook quick release). Print-in-place: no. Gear trains/gearboxes: yes in all three (serial, planetary, differential, worm, bevel, rack and pinion, automotive transmissions). Powered connectors: Slocum covers magnetic circuits, permanent-magnet attraction, solenoids and electromagnetically applied clutches; no motorised locks. Adhesives: Slocum has a page on adhesive joints comparing PVA white glue (solvent evaporation, porous surfaces), cyanoacrylate super glue (moisture-cured, not for porous surfaces, bonds rubber and metal), two-part epoxy (laminates, gap filling, thread locking), UV-cured adhesives and thread-locking agents, with joint geometry ratings; the Navy book has none; UArk joining chapter may cover adhesives [uncertain]
coverage.entry_structure: Slocum: two-page spread per topic, one page of detailed text and one page of a colour photo collage with bullet notes, thought exercises in red italics, and a linked Excel design spreadsheet. Navy: narrative chapter sections with numbered line drawings, worked examples with numbers, and a quiz. UArk: web chapters with text and figures [uncertain]
coverage.audience_level: Slocum: advanced high school to university (the author suggests using it for FIRST robot teams); UArk: undergraduate; Navy: school level / enlisted sailors with no engineering background

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: Navy: high, written for sailors with no engineering background, plain language, everyday examples and simple arithmetic. Slocum: medium, the picture pages are very approachable but the text pages use university-level mechanics and many puns. UArk: medium, a standard introductory undergraduate textbook [uncertain]
usefulness.has_images: yes: Slocum has full-colour photo collages and CAD renderings on every other page (good quality, but small and busy); Navy has clear black-and-white line drawings (good quality, older scan quality varies); UArk has figures [uncertain]
usefulness.has_animations: no animations in the books; Slocum's page links 2006-2007 online lecture videos that require RealPlayer 8 (a dead format, not checked) [uncertain]
usefulness.gaps: No index by function or behaviour, no plain-English lookup by what you want to achieve, nothing specific to 3D printing, snap fits or print-in-place, no CAD files; Slocum is dated (2008) and all rights reserved; the Navy book is 1940s-1960s technology (typewriters, ship machinery) and not organised around connections at all; the UArk book could not be opened from this environment
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: moderately: the Navy book is best as a public-domain source of diagrams to copy (not link); Slocum's chapter PDFs have stable URLs (e.g. https://pergatory.mit.edu/resources/FUNdaMENTALs%20Book%20pdf/FUNdaMENTALs%20Topic%205.PDF for clutches, couplings and interference fits) but links go to a whole 60-page chapter, so entries would have to cite a page number; UArk Pressbooks chapters have per-chapter URLs [uncertain]
usefulness.reusable_data: Navy: fully reusable (public domain), with OCR text and PDFs on the Internet Archive. UArk: reusable non-commercially with attribution (CC BY-NC). Slocum: not reusable (all rights reserved), link only; the Excel spreadsheets are downloadable but no licence is given
usefulness.maintained: Slocum: online and working (chapter PDFs and the 51 MB zip downloaded fine) but frozen since 2008; the linked lecture videos use RealPlayer. UArk: current (2024) but its host was blocked from here, so availability was not checked directly [uncertain]. Navy: frozen historical documents, preserved on the Internet Archive
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) Slocum's 'picture page first' idea: let readers browse a collage of photos, then read the detail for whatever catches their eye, which suits people who do not know the terms. (2) Slocum's advice to 'turn over the whole box of parts' before choosing, i.e. show all the options in a family side by side. (3) The Navy book's method of explaining a complex device as a chain of simple machines ('start where the energy goes in and follow it step by step'), which could be a tip on each entry. (4) Use everyday examples (hatch dogs, capstans, jacks) to explain a principle before naming it. (5) Pair each type with a small calculator, as Slocum does with spreadsheets. (6) Reuse the public-domain Navy line drawings for gear, clutch, coupling, ratchet and detent entries
usefulness.design_rules_given: yes in Slocum: worked design spreadsheets with numbers for interference fits (e.g. required interference in micrometres and interface pressure), shafts (axial, torsion, bending, stability), belts and cable wraps (safety factor 1.2 against slip), leadscrew efficiency (30 to 50 percent for leadscrews, about 95 percent for ballscrews), gears, bolted joints, bearings and flexures; adhesive lap shear strength about 15 MPa and epoxy shrinkage 0.2 percent constrained / 5 percent unconstrained. Navy: mechanical advantage formulas and worked examples. UArk: unknown [uncertain]
usefulness.generator_or_parametric: Slocum provides downloadable Excel design spreadsheets per chapter (linkages, power transmission, screws and gears, motors/springs/pistons, structures, interfaces, bearings, precision engineering); not geometry generators. Others: none
usefulness.file_formats: PDF (Slocum chapters and a whole-book zip; Navy scans with OCR text, EPUB for the 1971 edition; UArk PDF, eBook and XML per the Open Textbook Library), Excel XLS spreadsheets (Slocum), web pages (UArk)
usefulness.terminology_value: medium: good for proper names of classic machine elements (Oldham coupling, sprag clutch, kinematic coupling, quasi-kinematic coupling, elastic averaging, toggle, detent, escapement, pelican hook), and the Navy book gives plain-English equivalents ('blocks - pulleys to a landlubber'); no translations
usefulness.decision_support: Little: Slocum gives the FRDPARRC design table method (functional requirements, design parameters, analysis, references, risks, countermeasures) and comparison ratings for adhesive joint geometries (butt OK, lap good, scarf excellent); the Navy book has none; UArk teaches concept selection methods in general [uncertain]
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: Original works. Slocum draws on his Precision Machine Design and MIT 2.007; the Navy Basic Machines overlaps with other Navy training manuals and the Dover reprint; all three overlap with standard machine design textbooks (Shigley, Norton) and with Wikipedia articles on the same elements. The UArk book is listed in the Open Textbook Library
